title: 42 Prompts to Get Students Speaking or Writing at the Start of the School Year https://davestuartjr.com/42-prompts-to-get-students-speaking-or-writing-at-the-start-of-the-school-year
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart shares a set of 42 relationship-building writing/discussion prompts he plans to use as classroom warm-ups at the start of the school year, framed by his belief that connection with students is best built through, not instead of, content and skill work. The prompts range from playful and personal (favorite foods, weirdest gifts) to more reflective (people who've shaped you, values, aspirations), giving teachers a spread of options for different moods and purposes. He closes with three practical notes: circulate the room to ensure written warm-ups are treated as non-optional, use quiet acknowledgment to signal warmth while students write, and always invite a few students to share aloud so peers feel heard. Stuart's underlying claim is that the specific prompts matter less than the consistency and intentionality of how a teacher uses them to build relationship inside the normal work of class.
points: Stuart frames relationship-building as something that happens "in the context of" academic work rather than as a separate, competing activity — a "connection AND content" stance rather than "connection over content."
The list mixes whimsical prompts (tattoos, weird food combos) with reflective ones (role models, historical dinner guests) so teachers can match tone to the moment.
He insists written warm-ups must be signaled as non-negotiable early in the year, with the teacher actively circulating rather than treating the time as a break.
Genuine listening when students share aloud is positioned as the real payoff of the exercise — it communicates to the whole class that individuals are seen and enjoyed.
quotes: I'm not as much a "connection over content" guy as I am a "connection AND content" guy. In my high school classes, relationship building is most often done in the context of skill or knowledge building.

There's a whole essay I could write on why I'm that way, but that's not the point today. The point is that when my students come into the classroom, the most common thing they'll see on the projector screen is a set of writing prompts.
Often, at least one of these prompts is personal/whimsical/"connection"-oriented, and at least one of these prompts is academic/recall/"content"-oriented.

If you do these as a written warm-up, make sure you're circulating throughout the room and helping anyone who is stuck. Especially in the early weeks of school, you want to be sure you're signaling to students that written warm-ups are not optional.
At the same time, you can signal warmth during this writing time by silently acknowledging what you are seeing students write or quietly saying hello to students you may have missed at the door.
And always, ask for at least a couple of students to share. When students share, focus on really listening. You want to signal to them and their watching peers that you hear and enjoy who they are.
